title: Wireless & Mobile Networks
summary: No cable, no problem — until interference hits. Learn how WiFi, cellular, and mobile handoff work, and why wireless is fundamentally harder than wired.

blocks.markdown:
**Wireless networks** transmit data over radio waves instead of cables. That one change ripples through everything: the medium is shared, signals fade, devices move.

- **WiFi** is the dominant local wireless standard (IEEE 802.11).
- **Cellular** (3G/4G/5G) covers wide areas using towers.
- Key challenges: interference, limited bandwidth, mobility, security.
- Builds on [physical-data-link-layer](physical-data-link-layer) concepts.

blocks.subTitle: Wired vs wireless at a glance
blocks.markdown:
The core differences.

| Property | Wired | Wireless |
|---|---|---|
| Medium | Private cable | Shared air |
| Collision detect | Yes (CSMA/CD) | No — use avoidance |
| Signal quality | Stable | Varies with distance |

Shared air is the root of most wireless complexity.

Wired: each cable is a **private channel**. Wireless: all devices in range share the same radio frequency — the **shared medium** problem.

- **Interference** from microwaves, neighbors, or walls degrades signal.
- **No collision detection**: you can't listen and transmit simultaneously in wireless — radios can't hear their own signal while sending.
- **Hidden node problem**: two senders out of each other's range both think the channel is free and collide at the receiver.

blocks.subTitle: Standards and access points
blocks.markdown:
**WiFi** is defined by IEEE **802.11** standards. Devices connect to an **access point (AP)** — the radio base station — which bridges them to a wired network.

- **SSID** (Service Set Identifier): the human-readable network name you see in the list.
- Key standards: 802.11n (WiFi 4), 802.11ac (WiFi 5), 802.11ax (WiFi 6).
- Each generation adds more channels, wider bandwidth, smarter scheduling.
- **Infrastructure mode**: all traffic routes through the AP, not peer-to-peer.

blocks.subTitle: CSMA/CA — collision avoidance
blocks.markdown:
**CSMA/CA** (Carrier Sense Multiple Access / Collision **Avoidance**) is how WiFi manages the shared medium.

1. Listen — if the channel is busy, wait.
2. Wait a random **backoff** time after it goes idle.
3. Send. If a collision still happens, wait longer before retrying.

**ACK**: the receiver sends an acknowledgment; no ACK = retransmit. Avoidance is necessary because collision *detection* is impossible in wireless.

blocks.subTitle: CSMA/CD vs CSMA/CA
blocks.markdown:
Two different strategies for the same problem.

| | CSMA/CD (Ethernet) | CSMA/CA (WiFi) |
|---|---|---|
| Strategy | Detect collision, stop, retry | Avoid collision before sending |
| Feasible because | Can hear while sending | Cannot hear while sending |
| Overhead | Low | Higher (backoff + ACKs) |

See [physical-data-link-layer](physical-data-link-layer) for Ethernet collision domains.

blocks.subTitle: 2.4 GHz vs 5 GHz
blocks.markdown:
WiFi operates in two main **frequency bands** — each a different slice of radio spectrum with different physics.

- **2.4 GHz**: longer wavelength travels further, penetrates walls better. Only 3 non-overlapping channels. Heavy interference from microwaves and neighboring networks.
- **5 GHz**: shorter range, struggles through walls. ~25 non-overlapping channels. Much less congested, higher throughput.
- **WiFi 6E** adds the **6 GHz** band for even more clean spectrum.

blocks.subTitle: Trade-off table
blocks.markdown:
Pick the band by distance and density.

| | 2.4 GHz | 5 GHz |
|---|---|---|
| Range | Longer | Shorter |
| Wall penetration | Better | Weaker |
| Congestion | High | Low |

Rule of thumb: 2.4 GHz for range and coverage; 5 GHz for speed in the same room.

blocks.subTitle: Cells, generations, handoff
blocks.markdown:
Cellular networks divide geography into **cells**, each served by a **base station** (tower). Cells reuse frequencies because neighbors use different ones.

- **3G**: first usable mobile internet; circuit-switched voice + packet data.
- **4G LTE**: IP-only, ~10–100 Mbps, low latency for video and apps.
- **5G**: sub-ms latency targets, massive IoT support, mmWave for dense areas.
- **Handoff**: when your device moves from one cell to another, the network seamlessly transfers the connection — invisible to you when it works.

- Smaller cells = more base stations = higher capacity per km².

blocks.subTitle: WEP / WPA2 / WPA3
blocks.markdown:
Wireless signals broadcast to anyone in range — encryption is essential.

- **WEP** (Wired Equivalent Privacy): broken, crackable in minutes. Never use.
- **WPA2** (WiFi Protected Access 2): AES encryption, the current baseline. Use at minimum.
- **WPA3**: replaces WPA2's handshake with **SAE** (Simultaneous Authentication of Equals) — protects against offline dictionary attacks and adds forward secrecy.
- **Open networks**: no encryption; all traffic visible to anyone on the same AP.

Wireless is harder than wired in several systematic ways:

- **Signal attenuation**: strength drops with distance squared; walls cut it further.
- **Multipath fading**: reflected signals arrive at slightly different times and interfere with each other.
- **Mobility**: IP routing assumes fixed topology — mobile devices complicate routing, TCP, and connection state. See [network-performance-qos](network-performance-qos).
- **Higher latency variance**: retransmits, contention, and handoffs all add jitter.

blocks.subTitle: CSMA/CA vs CSMA/CD
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: Why does WiFi use CSMA/CA instead of CSMA/CD?**

Collision **detection** requires listening while transmitting. Wireless radios can't do this — a transmitting radio's own signal overwhelms anything it could receive. So WiFi uses collision **avoidance**: random backoff before sending, plus ACKs to confirm delivery. Detection is physically impossible; avoidance is the only option.

blocks.subTitle: 2.4 vs 5 GHz choice
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: When would you use 2.4 GHz vs 5 GHz WiFi?**

**2.4 GHz** for range and wall penetration — e.g. a device one room away or through thick walls. **5 GHz** for throughput and low congestion — e.g. streaming in the same room as the AP. The trade-off is physics: lower frequency = longer range, fewer channels; higher frequency = shorter range, more clean channels.

blocks.subTitle: Cellular handoff
blocks.markdown:
**Q: What is a handoff in cellular networks and why is it hard?**

A **handoff** (or handover) is the network transferring an active connection from one base station to another as the device moves. It's hard because the network must:
1. Detect weakening signal and choose a target cell.
2. Transfer connection state without dropping calls or resetting TCP.
3. Do it fast enough that the user doesn't notice.

Soft handoff (briefly connected to both) reduces drops; hard handoff cuts before connecting.

blocks.subTitle: Why wireless is less reliable
blocks.markdown:
**Q: Why is wireless inherently less reliable than wired?**

Three physical realities: (1) **shared medium** — all devices contend for the same channel; (2) **signal degradation** — walls, distance, interference weaken the signal, causing bit errors and retransmits; (3) **mobility** — devices change location, causing handoffs and route changes. Wired links have none of these: each cable is private, shielded, and the endpoints don't move.

blocks.subTitle: WPA2 vs WPA3
blocks.markdown:
**Q: What does WPA3 improve over WPA2?**

WPA2 uses a pre-shared key handshake (4-way) that is vulnerable to **offline dictionary attacks** — an attacker captures the handshake and tries passwords offline. WPA3 replaces this with **SAE** (dragonfly handshake), which prevents offline cracking even if the password is weak. WPA3 also provides **forward secrecy**: past sessions stay protected even if the key is later compromised.
